summary: Defines the syntax and semantics of relative Uniform Resource Locators, which let a reference inherit context from a known base URL instead of repeating everything. It was a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 3986.

plainLanguage.summary: A relative URL is a short way of writing an address inside a document. Instead of repeating the protocol, the host and the whole path, it says only what is different, and the reader works out the rest from the address of the document that holds it. This RFC defines what such a reference may look like, how to find the address to work from, and the exact steps that turn one into a full address.

questions: how do relative urls resolve against a base
how do dot dot segments work in urls
how is a relative url resolved
subtitle: How a short reference inside a document is turned back into a full address.

tldr.problem: A link written in full repeats information the reader already has: the scheme, the host and part of the path. It also ties a set of documents to one place, so moving them means editing every link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a syntax for relative references, rules for finding the base address a document is read against, and a seven-step algorithm that combines the two into an absolute URL, including the handling of the dot and dot-dot path segments.
tldr.outcome: A tree of documents can be moved or served under different schemes without changing the links inside it, and parsers can be tested against a common set of examples. The document was later replaced by RFC 3986.

today: RFC 1808 was published in June 1995 as a Proposed Standard. It was updated by RFC 2368 and RFC 2396, and it has since been obsoleted by RFC 3986.

sections.title: Why Write Addresses in Short Form
sections.content:
A URL is a compact representation of the location and the access method for a resource on the Internet. When a URL is embedded in a document, an absolute URL repeats a great deal of information that the context already supplies: the scheme, the network location and parts of the path. Where the base URL is well defined and known to the parser, whether a person or a program, it is useful to embed a reference that inherits that context instead of restating it. Relative URLs also shorten what a person has to type into a data-entry field.

Documents are often published as a group or tree serving one purpose, and most of the links inside them point within that tree rather than outside it. Relative addressing makes such a tree independent of where it sits and of how it is reached: the same set of hypertext documents can be accessible and traversable at the same time over the file, http and ftp schemes if the documents refer to each other relatively, and the whole tree can be moved without changing a single embedded URL. The RFC says experience with the World-Wide Web has shown that relative referencing is necessary for the long-term usability of embedded URLs.

The document is a companion to RFC 1738, which specifies absolute URLs. This one covers the syntax and semantics of relative URLs, and it also has to describe enough of the general URL syntax to explain how a relative reference is parsed and resolved.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the full address in every link repeats the protocol, the host and the path each time. A short reference says only what changes, and the reader works out the rest from the address of the document that contains it. That also lets a set of documents be moved, or served under a different protocol, without editing the links inside.

sections.title: The Parts of an Address
sections.content:
The syntax depends on the scheme: some schemes use characters such as ? and ; for special components, others treat them as ordinary path characters. There is enough uniformity, however, for a parser to resolve relative references against a single generic syntax, which has six components in a fixed order: <scheme>://<net_loc>/<path>;<params>?<query>#<fragment>. All of them except the scheme may be absent. The scheme is the name before the colon, the double slash introduces the network location and login information, the slash introduces the path, a semicolon introduces object parameters such as ;type=a, a question mark introduces query information, and a hash introduces the fragment identifier. When both parameters and a query are present, the query comes after the parameters.

The fragment identifier, and the hash that precedes it, are not part of the URL. Because a fragment is commonly written in the same string as a URL, a parser still has to recognise it and set it aside.

The RFC gives a BNF for the syntax. The essential rules are that a relative URL is a network path, an absolute path or a relative path; that a relative path is an optional path followed by optional parameters and an optional query; and that a path is a first segment followed by any number of further segments separated by slashes. Characters outside the allowed set may be written as an escape of the form % followed by two hexadecimal digits. Parsing runs in a fixed order: the fragment is taken off first, then the scheme, then the network location, then the query, then the parameters, and what is left is the path. The parser has to remember whether the path had a leading slash, because that is what separates an absolute path from a relative one.
sections.plainLanguage: Every address is built from the same pieces in the same order: a scheme, a host, a path, extra parameters, a query, and a fragment that points inside the resource. A relative reference is simply one of these pieces left out. A parser takes the pieces off in a fixed order, and the first thing it does is set aside the fragment.

sections.title: Finding the Address to Work From
sections.content:
A relative reference means nothing without an absolute base URL to apply it to, and the base URL of a document must be known to whoever parses it. There are four ways it can be established, listed in order of precedence, so that the innermost defined base URL wins.

The first is a base URL embedded in the document's own content. Some media types allow this, which is useful for descriptive documents such as tables of contents that may be sent to others by other means. How each media type embeds it is out of scope here. Messages are treated as composite documents, and the RFC recommends the header form Base: <URL:absoluteURL>, where Base is case-insensitive and any whitespace inside the angle brackets is ignored; for example Base: <URL:http://www.ics.uci.edu/Test/a/b/c>. The base URL of a message serves as the base for relative URLs in its headers and as the default base for documents enclosed within it.

The second is the base URL of the encapsulating entity. If nothing is embedded, the base URL of a document is defined by its retrieval context, and for a document enclosed within another entity that context is the entity itself. Composite media types such as multipart/* and message/* define a hierarchy of retrieval context, so the retrieval context of a part is the base URL of the composite entity it belongs to, and a base header in the composite redefines the context of its parts, recursively.

The third is the URL used to retrieve the document. If the retrieval resulted from a redirect, the base URL is the last URL used, the one that produced the actual retrieval. The fourth is the default: if none of the above applies, the base URL is the empty string and every embedded URL in the document is assumed absolute. The RFC puts the responsibility on whoever distributes a document to make sure a base URL can be established, and stresses that relative URLs cannot be used reliably where the base URL is not well defined.
sections.plainLanguage: A short reference is meaningless until you know the address it is relative to. There are four places that address can come from, and the most specific one wins: a base stated inside the document, the base of the message or file that encloses it, the address the document was fetched from, or, failing all of those, no base at all, in which case every reference must be a full address.

sections.title: Turning a Short Reference into a Full Address
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example algorithm for resolving a relative URL against a base URL so that the result is always in absolute form. Implementation is not required, since other methods may work better for a given system, but the algorithm lets implementations be tested against each other. It guarantees that any valid URL, relative or absolute, can be turned consistently into an absolute form given a valid base URL.

The first steps establish the base URL and parse both the base and the embedded URL into their component parts. If the base URL is the empty string, the embedded URL is taken as absolute and the process ends. If the embedded URL is entirely empty, it inherits the entire base URL. If it starts with a scheme name, it is absolute. Otherwise it inherits the scheme of the base URL, and, unless it carries its own network location, the network location of the base URL.

The path is then settled. If the embedded path starts with a slash it is not relative, and nothing more is inherited. If the embedded path is empty and has no leading slash, it inherits the path of the base URL, and then the parameters and the query are inherited if the embedded ones are empty. Otherwise the last segment of the base path is removed and the embedded path is put in its place, and four clean-up operations are applied in order: every occurrence of a ./ where the dot is a complete segment is removed; a trailing . segment is removed; every occurrence of a complete segment followed by /../ is removed, repeatedly, taking the leftmost match each time; and a trailing complete segment followed by /.. is removed.

The last step recombines the components, including any that were inherited. Two details are worth noting: parameters do not form part of the path, so a ;type=d parameter on an ftp URL does not affect how relative paths resolve; and fragment identifiers are inherited from the base URL only when the whole embedded URL is empty.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolution fills in the parts the short reference leaves out, one at a time: it takes the scheme, the host and, when needed, the folder part of the base address. The special segments . and .. are then applied, meaning the current folder and the folder above it. What comes out is a full address in exactly the same form as one written out by hand.

sections.title: Worked Examples and Good Practice
sections.content:
The RFC resolves every example against one base address, http://a/b/c/d;p?q#f. In the normal cases, g becomes http://a/b/c/g, because the last segment of the base path is replaced; /g becomes http://a/g, because a leading slash starts at the root; //g becomes http://g, because it carries its own host; ?y becomes http://a/b/c/d;p?y, because it changes only the query; #s becomes http://a/b/c/d;p?q#s, because it changes only the fragment; and .. becomes http://a/b/. A reference that carries a scheme of its own, such as g:h, is left alone and becomes g:h.

The RFC also lists abnormal cases that parsers should still handle consistently. An empty reference resolves to the complete base URL. When there are more .. segments than the base path has levels, the extras stay in place, so ../../../g becomes http://a/../g, and the .. syntax can never change the host. The dot and dot-dot names are only special when they make up a whole segment: /./g becomes http://a/./g and g. becomes http://a/b/c/g.. The older form that keeps the base scheme in the reference, as in http:g, is described as a loophole in earlier specifications of partial URLs that future parsers should avoid.

For authors, the RFC recommends that a path name containing a colon cannot be the first component of a relative path, because it will be taken for a scheme name; such a path has to be preceded by other components, as in ./this:that, or have the colon escaped as this%3Athat, and the first solution is preferred because it does not affect the absolute form. For ftp, the RFC recommends not using the ;type=d parameter where relative URLs are allowed, because a trailing slash in the base path is what tells a reader that the location is a directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC works through a list of examples against a single base address, so that two programs can be compared on the same cases. Two traps are worth knowing: a name that begins with a colon-looking prefix is mistaken for a scheme, and a dot or dot-dot only counts when it is a whole segment of the path.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is brief here: there are no security considerations in the use or parsing of relative URLs. Once a relative URL has been resolved to its absolute form, the same security considerations apply as those described for absolute URLs in RFC 1738.

One consequence follows from the base URL rules rather than from the parsing rules. Because the base URL decides where every relative reference in a document points, a document whose base URL cannot be established cannot use relative references reliably. That is why the RFC puts the responsibility for supplying a base URL on whoever distributes the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Relative references carry no security risks of their own. Once one has been turned into a full address, the usual rules for that kind of address apply. The thing to watch is the base address: if it is unclear where a document came from, its relative links cannot be trusted to point where the author meant.
